items.text: I agree with Misti Y--. Some people will love the Cirque shows and not really like Le Reve. This is a separate discussion. For me the theatre is the best part. The design and the decor is simply stunning from beginning to end. The concept behind the show is really beautiful and appealing. It doesn't translate to the actual show very well. The story isn't that entertaining. On the show that I saw, the stage kept breaking down all night. It was hard to stay engaged in it, even during the impressive scenes. Le Reve tries to reach for the flashiness and spectacle of Cirque, but never really achieves it. It's mostly for the chance to go see the beautiful theatre. Otherwise you might be better off putting your money into another show.

Bought this keyboard from a marketplace. Mechanical keyboard. $38. I think I got $38 worth of keyboard. Maybe a bit more.
The space bar rattles. Every time I press my thumbs on it it goes clatter clatter. Like a tray of cutlery being nudged. You tune it out during the day, but after midnight I find myself typing around it. The "E" key also repeats now and then, so "meeting" becomes "meeeting". It happens maybe once every few paragraphs. Rare enough to forget. Frequent enough that I reread everything before I hit send.
I messaged the seller to ask what switches it used. I got tired of waiting and bought it anyway. Answer came a week later, after the keyboard was already on my desk. Brown switches, for the record.
The comfort is why I'm keeping it. Each key has a small bump partway down. So my fingers know a press registered without slamming to the bottom. I can get through a long email and my wrists feel fine afterward, which the flat laptop keys never managed.
I thought about sending it back. Return shipping would have eaten a real chunk of what I paid. And I'd be back on the laptop. So it stays, rattle and all.

I went to this circus theatre show in Vegas and I'm pretty keen on it. I'd give it 4 stars. Storyline's a bit hard to follow, and some of the songs feel boring or the wrong fit for the action. But the performers are great. Really impressive athleticism, great physiques, super fit. The women are amazing. They'll stay underwater for a few minutes at a time.

The theatre is round, and the stage is round too. So you get a good view no matter where you sit. There's three main entrances for the stage, and they're key for the big scene changes. Stage, set, lights, it's all really pretty and really sets a good vibe.

Tickets are not expensive compared to O or Love. I just wish there was more spectacle, more fire. But not a big deal. Story and music are issues, but it's a fun show, really pretty, and I do recommend it.

Remote work gets pushed as a cure-all, but in two years of mentoring five junior engineers, I think it's really overblown for juniors who are still learning to code.

Jrs don't really need tickets or docs or meetings. They need to be in on design conversations. They need to see how people debug things, and ask questions before they're lost for hours. That kind of stuff just happens naturally in the office. If you're remote, they need to know when it's ok to cut in or ask to set up a call and explain a problem they don't fully get yet. For a junior, that's a skill, and a really hard one to be expected to have before you get to learn it.

I've seen the feedback problems in remote work. A short code review comment can land like the final word instead of a chance to learn. It also takes longer, so you lose momentum. The juniors I mentored improved faster with in person pairing, whiteboard sessions, easy access to seniors. I'm not pushing to force people back into offices. Remote work can be great for self-driven devs. But for juniors, being close to people is a booster. It gives you confidence, context, and instincts. If you just send a junior off with a laptop and a calendar, it can really drag junior development. Down the line, you'll get less good technical leadership.

So it's 3:17 AM. The mixer is just there, humming its steady drone and the vibration is coming right through the soles of my boots. The flour dust is all in the air, catching the harsh fluorescent light. It's almost like suspended snow. My hands are wiped down on the apron, its fabric is stiff from dried dough and sweat. I went over to the front counter to check the lock. It's just a ritual, born of paranoia.

And there it sat. The History of Salt. It's a hardback with a blue spine that's cracked near the hinge. This book has been appearing every Thursday for six weeks, always placed precisely on the glass display case next to the unsold cinnamon rolls. It doesn't have a library stamp on it that would say it belongs here, and it's not a branch of the municipal library system. So I picked it up. The cover felt cold. I opened it expecting blank pages or maybe a forgotten bookmark. But a folded square of lined notebook paper slipped out and landed on the counter with a soft tap.

I unfolded it. The handwriting was jagged, pressed hard into the fiber. It said "You knead with your left hand dominant, stop favoring the right. It ruins the tension." The mixer ticked over to the next cycle. I looked down at my hands, red knuckled and dusted white. I closed the book and put it back on the glass display case, aligning the spine perfectly with the edge. Then I turned off the overhead light above the display and just left the book in shadow.

So from personal experience, Apple deserves a mention. My school only let us Apple users in middle and high school, even though they cost about 2x a PC. Those laptops would break monthly. I never once dropped my laptop, but I replaced the hard drive five times over four years and had to reinstall the OS again and again. One time, my friend's MacBook Pro caught fire while he was watching a movie, and the smoke alarm went off. And Apple support could not diagnose the problem, but just backed up, wiped and restored files. It gets even worse with iPhones. My first iPhone was broken a lot. Now Apple puts out a new iPhone every two months or so. The difference from the previous model is only a slightly better camera. And yes, I admit iPads are the best tablets now, but maybe Androids will catch up.

It is a good show, but not a must see at wynn las vegas. So not something I'd go to vegas for.

I've been taken to vegas constantly since I was a kid, and I have seen a lot of shows before I was 21. So I know what it can be.

Good news, the circular stage is a really smart idea. From any seat it's great, which is super rare in these big theatre shows. If you stay at the wynn or encore, you can get a good deal. Tickets are 125, and if you're a hotel guest, they're 99.

Some of the individual acts are really impressive, and the performers are good as hell. Aerialists, acrobats, whatever. But so many of the feats are things I've seen in Cirque du Soleil, and done just as well.

The real problem is the story. It's unclear, it's weak, or not really there. I left not really knowing what it was trying to say. Also too much happening at once. Too many visuals, too many moving things, too many wow attempts. It would hit harder if it was more restrained.

Other than a few cool stunts, it's pretty average. I wasn't blown away. Nobody I was with was blown away. Some friends liked it, so I'd say go check it out if you haven't, especially with the wynn/encore deal. But I wouldn't see it again, or pay full price to see it again. It's the stereotypical vegas spectacle, where big and more means better. But more was just more messy for me.

So I recently bought a skateboard at Zumiez and went back for the rest of the gear. First impressions were fine. Me, my friend, and his little brother were chatting with a lady, who said she's the manager. Said she's been assembling boards daily throughout her employment. Said she once was having a bad day and was annoyed and mistreated customers or people. Then assembly took like 90 minutes. I thought 15. She stripped two bolts, then replaced them in a way that seemed like she'd sell them to another customer. Finally, she brought in her brother and another employee, also a manager, to help finish it. No apology. Zumiez has lost our future business. My heart was crushed.

Picked up a mechanical keyboard second hand for 38 bucks. Its been a messy but good experience. The guy selling it was bad on communication, I asked him what switch it had before I bought it. He replied to my message a week later with one word. At that point, I already took a gamble and ordered it. So I waited. The keyboard is very used. The space bar rattles like a loose Lego brick, its really annoying. The E key double types. So theee, instead of the, its hilarious. But I really enjoy typing on it. The feedback is very good, the tactile is really good. And I type long emails, its really comfortable for me. And they are long painful work emails. But I really enjoy it. I was thinking of returning it, but it's a heavy slab of plastic, and shipping is a pain. For 38, not worth the hassle. And now I really like it. Even the flaws. If you're willing to do some DIY tuning and a letter double typing now and then, its a good deal.

I really want to warn folks about Turkish Airlines. Took the domestic Harbin to Beijing flight and then booked Turkish Airlines to Istanbul. My flight from Harbin was delayed, so I missed the connection. When I went to the booth at the airport, they didn't take responsibility or rebook me. I spent the night there. Morning I asked for a ticket, staff told me flights were overbooked, it'd take days to get to Istanbul unless I paid business class. But I needed to get to Istanbul, so I had no choice and accepted business. Still in disbelief, and pretty angry.

So bring just one broken household item and get it fixed. When you get there, go to the registration desk, get a ticket, and keep it safe because that number gives you your spot in the queue. Repairs are done by volunteers and it's first-come first-served, and you need to pick up your stuff before they leave at 4:00. We don't store things overnight. Make sure you have enough time to wait your turn. We can't promise they'll be able to fix all devices. Thanks for following these simple procedures to keep the session running smoothly.

The float valve controls filling of the trough. It has a buoyant float attached to a valve. When water level drops, the float drops and opens valve so water can enter. As the water rises, the float rises and slowly closes the valve. At the set level the valve shuts off and stops filling. Two normal causes of overflow are debris or minerals clogging the valve from closing fully, or the float being set too high so it doesn't close until the trough is already overflowing.

I really can't even tell you if the food was good. We never got to eat. We got there 7:20 PM on Sunday. We picked this place because we had a 10 PM show at the same hotel, and figured it'd be easy. We put our names on the digital waitlist which is completely useless. Told us to come back and pay at 8:23 PM. Did, but then we stood around until 8:40 PM before staff casually said we might not be seated until 9:15. Just two people. They offered zero solutions. If the wait is going to be that far past payment, please tell people up front so our night doesn't get completely wasted. Absolute disaster. Zero stars if it were an option.

To all Enron employees,

I know these are hard days. Enron's problems are bad enough already and add the world's bad news and holidays don't feel like holidays.

We talked a lot about the Enron party on Dec 8. Some people were in favor. It's a good chance for us to celebrate. Other folks thought it was not appropriate. I get it.

Given the whole month, we have decided to cancel it. Spending corporate money on a party right now could be viewed as imprudent. This is a risk we don't want to take.

I'm sorry. You have worked hard. You deserve recognition and a reason to celebrate. We'll find other ways to show you how much your great contributions mean to us over the holidays.

Ken Lay

A siphon moves water between two containers using gravity and air pressure. The tube is filled with water first so there is one continuous column. Gravity pulls the water down the longer, downhill side toward the lower container. That pull makes a partial vacuum at the top. Air pressure then pushes on the source water and pushes more liquid up the shorter side to fill that low pressure. This is what keeps the flow going.

The outlet has to be lower than the source water surface. The driving force is the weight difference between the two columns. If the outlet is level or higher, there is not enough downward force to get the water up the intake. There is a net gravitational pull only when the column on the exit side is heavier than the rising one.

Air is the killer here. If air gets into the tube, it breaks the continuous column and the chain of molecules that passes the suction. So it equalizes the pressure inside the tube with the outside atmosphere and kills the pressure difference. The whole thing stops. The tube has to be primed again and filled full of liquid.

Sourdough was on its second rise and I found it again. It’s always a Thursday, always right on the flour bin, always that copy of The Count of Monte Cristo with the Richmond Public Library stamp. I don't know how they get past the squeaky screen door without me hearing them. Frankly at 3:00 AM my brain is mostly yeast and caffeine anyway. But tonight a scrap of yellow legal paper was poking out of the top like a bookmark. I wiped my hands on my apron, leaving a ghostly white smudge on the dark cloth, and pulled it out. It said page 142 in frantic spiky handwriting. Please, it read. I think they’re watching the drop box now. A cold draft swept through the kitchen smelling of wet asphalt and oncoming rain. I looked toward the darkened front windows but all I saw was my own tired reflection staring back. I didn't open the book. Instead I carefully tucked the note back between the pages and slid the novel into a brown pastry bag. I folded the top down twice to seal it.

I spent $38 on a used mechanical keyboard and got about $38 worth of keyboard, maybe a little more. Let me start with the flaws. The spacebar rattles, not a gentle click, a hollow loose clatter every time my thumb hits it, like you push a tray of cutlery. I stopped noticing it during the day but at night it sounds louder than it has any right to. The E key also repeats itself sometimes, so meeting becomes meeeeting. Happens maybe once every few paragraphs. So it's just often enough to make me proofread. Communication with the seller was slow. I asked what switches it was before buying, got a reply a week later. It was brown switches. Still, the surprise is that it's actually comfortable to type on. Cushioned feeling, I can write long emails without my wrists complaining. Which is more than I can say for the flat laptop keyboard I had. I thought about returning it but the hassle didn't seem worth it. So it stays on my desk. It rattles, repeats, and quietly earns its keep. Three stars.

Hi everyone. Some of you know me, others don't. I'm Tom's brother, the one he shared a bunk bed with until he was 14. Since we grew up so close, I've seen his snoring and the fights over who gets the top bunk. I've also seen early signs that he'd become the incredibly reliable man we're celebrating today.

I can always count on Tom. Once I forgot my passport and he drove six hours to bring it to me. That's just the brother he is. Loyal, generous, and he'll go a completely unreasonable distance to save you from your own stupidity.

So Tom, I really do seem to have found someone who loves you like we do and, unlike me, decided to room with you on a voluntary basis.

I wasn't that into Cirque du Soleil, so Le Reve was my first. I expected to see a ton of backflips and acrobatics, but there was actually less acrobatics and more interpretive dancing. Their skills were really impressive, it just wasn't really my thing. Unbiased rating is 4 stars, but my personal rating is 2.5 stars. Anyone who likes theatrical spectacle will probably like Le Reve. But I wouldn't spend over $100 on these shows. I got free tickets, so I was very glad I didn't have to pay.

Old school attendance registers let historians see patterns of daily life that official records often miss. They show which kids showed up, how regular they were, and sometimes why they didn't. From that, you can figure out things like seasonal work needs, sickness, bad weather, poverty, home duties, moving around, or local emergencies. The registers also show differences by gender, age, neighborhood, or social class, so you see how schooling fit into work, household routines, and what the community expected. Look across lots of years and you see changes in schooling habits and public health.

The limit is that registers only record what the school chose to write down. They don't really explain what the kids were going through, and absences might be misreported or incomplete, or just reflect teacher assumptions. So they're most useful when compared with other sources.

2:17 every Thursday morning, Mara would find this library book on the back step of the bakery. Always the same one: A Field Guide to North American Moths, a county library sticker ghost-pale on the spine, a little flour worked into the jacket, as if the book had been helping. She had returned it twice. The librarians smiled too politely. By the third week, she kept it beside her rye starter and said nothing about it.

Tonight rain ticked against the alley door. The ovens were breathing. Mara was shaping croissants, her palms pressing butter into the dough, when the latch gave its tiny guilty click. No one was there, just the book, dry as a bone on the wet concrete. She wiped her hands on her apron and opened it. A slip of paper was between “Luna Moth” and “Promethea,” folded once. Your window is the only light on this street, it said. I read here until the first bus. I’m sorry about the crumbs.

Mara looked at the alley, the dented milk crates, steam rising off the drains. For a second the city felt enormous, then not. She tore a corner off an order pad and wrote, Cinnamon rolls come out at 4:05. She set the note inside the book, placed it on the warm windowsill, and unlocked the back door.

In our classroom project we tested how stable different folded cardboard bridges are. We made short beam, arch inspired, and triangular fold designs from the same cardboard, trying to keep the length and width as consistent as possible. Each one sat between two supports and we added small weights slowly, watching for bending, tipping, or collapse. Since it was handmade, we only had a small number of trials and the testing was just classroom conditions, you shouldn't treat the results like real engineering data. But in this activity, the triangular fold designs seemed to hold weight more steadily. It does seem like fold geometry can influence how stable these model bridges are.

The book was under the bench, by the back door where the bread peels hang. There's a steel table there. It's *A Field Guide to Coastal Birds*. The library stamp inside says due in March. The mail slot is nailed shut, been for years, but the hatch next to it doesn't latch properly. The flour man used to use it. Eleventh Thursday I checked it. I asked staff, looked for scratches, stayed late once, coat on. Nothing. The book would show up between two and four. I was at the ovens, back to the door.

Tonight, receipt from Pell's folded into oystercatchers page. Ink was blotchy, someone pressed hard. Note says: "I keep meaning to take this back to the library. Then I pass your door and there's the smell of bread and I put it down instead. I can stop if you want." I smell salt. The pages did. She got a pencil out of her apron. Wrote: "Bring it Thursday. I'll have a roll." Tucked receipt back in, book on the hatch ledge. Warm roll in a paper bag beside it.

I live in Toronto now, don't use Hydro Ottawa, but I want to warn other consumers about their billing practices. I used to have an account for a year, was renting a downtown apartment. Moved back in with my parents for my MA. Cancelled account properly, paid all charges. But they kept siphoning payments from my other bank account at random intervals for over a year. I called customer service repeatedly, sent proof of the withdrawals. Reps said my account was closed and no debits were happening. We figured it out when my parents and I looked through our utility bills. They had linked my banking details to my parents' billing number because I said I moved back home. My parents didn't notice because they kept getting overpayment refunds, so the credits seemed normal. After hours on the phone and many different reps, a manager investigated, confirmed the error, and fixed it. Weirdly, they refused to refund me at first and just offered an apology. Never again will I give banking details for automatic debit. The way they use your data is just reckless and it should worry all of us.

3:40 am, second rye batch still proofing. Marisol noticed the book again. A library book on the flour bin near the back door. The plastic cover was cold, it had been in the alley. It's been happening every Thursday now, four times in a row. Same book: *A Field Guide to Night Birds*. It's stamped Eastgate Branch and overdue by 3 weeks. Every Thursday she'd put it in the drop box on her way home. But every Thursday it would come back, like the building is borrowing it.

She wiped her hands on her apron, opened the book. A folded index card fell out of the barn owls page. It read: You leave the vent fan on. The alley smells like bread until 5. I walk my mother's dog then, because she can't anymore. I keep forgetting to return this. Maybe I keep not wanting to. Signed R.

Marisol read it twice, oven timer counting down. Outside, the fan hummed, pushing warm air into the dark. She turned the card over. With the same grease pencil she used to mark trays, she wrote: *Rye's out at 4:15*. Then she tore a heel off yesterday's loaf, wrapped it in wax paper, put the book on top, and propped the back door open one inch.

I used Ryanair back when I was a broke student. My ex lived in Sweden and it was the cheapest way to get there. Terrible experience. At the airport they confiscated my £20 L’Occitane shower gel and said it was over the liquid limit, but it wasn’t. Told me to go buy a 100ml bottle at the airport pharmacy and I’d get it back. So I went, came back, and no one had any idea what I was on about. Great. £20 down the drain and I was furious. On top of that they fined me £5 at the gate because I had a water bottle in my cabin baggage, and I’d bought it inside the airport. Ryanair’s later dropped the Liverpool John Lennon to Stockholm Skavsta route so I fly Norwegian now. Their customer service is bad as well, funny, but their planes are newer and less old than Ryanair’s.

Not just you. I had a really wet Tuesday and then by Thursday I noticed my Brandywines splitting. You can see the seam down the side. Its that old story, dry then sudden rain. The insides drink up water faster than the skin can stretch. My Sungolds are mostly ok but a few look like they may follow. Once weather does this you cant really help it. The only thing I do to help is I keep my 2 day schedule more evenly. It doesn't really matter once the sky decides to do it all at once. You should be able to get a good crop of the rest of the vine. Pick the split ones off and use them for something else. Its more of a pain with the Brandywines. That thick skin is a liability in a storm like this. You may get more luck with Sungolds if you can keep them from taking so much water at once.

The College Board's hypocrisy is absolutely ridiculous. My friend did a one-hour SAT subject test and the proctor gave their room about 20 extra minutes. My friend is a stickler for integrity and knew it broke the standardized nature of the test, so she reported it through the hotline so no one else can do it. The outcome? Pure institutional unfairness. They went through an "investigation" and said there wasn't enough proof of misconduct to blame the proctor or other students. Yet they somehow found enough proof to say my friend was wrong and canceled her scores. It's weird to punish the person who reported the issue and let the people who actually made the mistake off.

It's always Thursdays. It shows up not on the counter. But wedged behind the flour bins by the back door. It's the same book, *A Field Guide to North American Moths*, Elmwood Branch. The due date is stamped so old the ink has turned violet. And I've never seen anyone leave it. By the time I'm elbow-deep in rye dough at two, I wouldn't notice a marching band.

For the first few weeks I just set it on the shelf by the register, and by Friday morning it was gone. Thursday, it's back. Fine. People are strange. I'm the guy who talks to his sourdough starter, so I'm not judging.

Tonight there's a note tucked at page 114, the luna moths. It says they only live a week. They don't even eat. I keep thinking that's a waste of a beautiful thing. Do you ever get to see the bread before it's gone? No signature, just pencil, pressed hard.

I read it twice, then a third time while the ovens ticked. Then I pulled the first loaf of the night. It's still crackling. I wrapped it in brown paper and set it behind the flour bins.

Its possible to feel suffocated in a room even when its a comfortable temperature. This is because temperature is only one part of comfort. Humidity is the problem. When its high, it slows down evaporation of moisture from your skin. That makes the air feel heavy. Its also about airflow. If air is not moving, carbon dioxide and odors and heat just hang around. That makes the room feel stuffy. Air conditioning can cool the air but it does not mean it will reduce humidity or move the air. Opening a window or running a fan or ventilation can help. It moves the air and lowers the moisture.

The idea of remote work is sold to us as a win-win. But after mentoring five junior engineers for two years, I don't think it works for them. They don't need a lot of tickets, documentation, or a bunch of scheduled meetings. What they need is just to get in on design arguments, to watch someone else get through a nasty bug, and get answers before a little uncertainty snowballs. You get all of that for free in an office. Work from home and they have to figure out when to interrupt, get a call set up, and explain a problem they probably don't understand yet. That is a pretty steep thing to ask of someone who hasn't had the chance to learn it.

I've watched that setup screw up feedback. A short note on a code review ends up reading like a final judgment, and the lag on getting answers kills any forward motion. The people I worked with moved ahead a lot quicker when they could pair up in person, work through things on a whiteboard, and actually get hold of the seniors. None of this means you should scrap flexibility. It works fine for people who can direct their own efforts. But for a beginner, being around other people is what gets them there. That's how they pick up the confidence, context, and judgment they are going to need. You are going to end up with weaker technical leadership down the road if you just hand a newcomer a laptop and a calendar.

So, simple rain gauges are just open tops on a narrow tube. It measures the rain with a top, and it will give you the rainfall depth. It's the depth of water that would have covered a flat ground if no evaporation, no drainage or no soak in. And it's usually in millimetres or inches. So we use a funnel. This funnel is like a wide top opening into a very narrow tube. Because it's narrow, it's easier to measure very small amounts of rain. So the tube has a scale that already accounts for the ratio of the areas. So if I read the tube, I get the true rainfall depth. Then wind is a source of error, it can cause the rain to go past the top opening, so we are undercounting. And then evaporation or splashing before I read it, so the rain that is falling on the ground before I measure it, it can distort the result.

Bought this keyboard used for $38. It seemed fair once I got it out of the box. There was a bit of dust between keys, and the caps had some shiny spots. For a secondhand board, not too bad.

What I really like about this is that it's really comfy. I write long emails for work. My hands feel less cramped than my office keyboard, which is really flat and not great. Switches have a consistent feel. Not too heavy. Case doesn't move around on desk.

What I don't like is that the spacebar rattles every time I hit it. It's a big clack. You can hear it during the quiet of the morning. And the E key randomly repeats if I type fast, so I get "neeed". Not every time, but enough that I'm really proofing everything more carefully.

I asked the seller what switches this has. Didn't reply till a week later. Had already received the board by then. Not the best.

But it's $38 and I'm keeping it. I felt it wasn't worth the trouble of shipping it back.

So at the repair cafe you can bring one broken item. You check in at the front table, you'll get a ticket. You hold on to that until your item is ready. They'll call out numbers in order. Some fixes will need your input or a quick decision, so stay close. Not everything can be fixed, they'll say, parts might need ordering or a repair won't be possible. Pick up your stuff before volunteers leave at 4:30, because if you don't claim it, they won't store it.

Went there Friday around 4:30pm, no line, which was pleasant. Two of us ate for around $130 and it was steep. I went in thinking it was about the same as steak house. It was actually a bit more than I expected. Honestly, disappointed that there was no steak. At that price I felt there should have been some steak. The meats were lamb, prime rib and chicken, all of which I feel can be found at other buffet in Las Vegas and for much less money. Seafood station had Alaskan crab legs and rock crab claws. Alaskan crab is found at a lot of buffets in Vegas, but I hadn't seen rock crab claws at other buffets, so it was interesting. No crab cracker was available, staff said wooden mallets were available but our table was so close to the next table that I didn't want to start smashing shells and pieces flying at next table. So, I just ate the crab legs. Asian station was not distinctive. Reminded me of Rampart buffet a lot. Dessert was gelato and pastries, nothing stood out. Also had fresh juice but didn't try. In general, acceptable but overpriced for what it offers. Worth trying if you are curious. But if there is a long line, I'd reconsider.

Old attendance registers are super useful to historians who want to see how people actually lived. They show daily life by tracking which students turned up. You can see patterns. Harvest time and flu seasons, or really bad weather, and you can see how these things changed attendance. One year kids might have been pulled off school to help the harvest, or if a flu broke out in the area, you'll see attendance drop off. Or kids just don't come for long stretches. This can highlight differences in social and cultural attitudes to school. But we have to be careful. Registers can be tampered with. Sometimes teachers or headmasters might have just written that kids were in class when they were not. Because of funding targets or just to avoid trouble from the education authorities. And it's quite rare that you get the reason for an absence. You need to go and look at other historical evidence to explain it. So, registers are useful but you have to be careful with them.

Apple deserves a mention, from personal experience. My school only allowed Apple computers for middle and high schoolers. They cost about twice as much as alternatives and would break like once a month. I never dropped my laptop. But I changed the hard drive 5 times in 4 years and reinstalled the OS many times. It's a float valve connecting troughs to a pressurised water line. Usually there's a float, a plastic ball or block. It floats on the water and is connected to the lever arm. So when the cows drink, the water level drops, the float sinks, the lever arm tips and it pulls the plunger, washer, whatever, away from the seat. So it opens and the water flows into the trough. As it fills, the float lifts. So it pushes the plunger back, closes the seat, and the opening gets smaller and smaller. And then it closes. When it starts to overflow, it's usually a worn or dirty washer. Or the float is punctured or waterlogged, so it's not lifting enough to close the valve. So it just keeps flowing and overflows.
